newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Primakov says coup in Russia "impossible".
newsitem.headline: Primakov says coup in Russia "impossible".

text.p: Russia's Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Monday dismissed as "impossible" the idea of a coup in Moscow and said the country no longer had to fear any attempt to seize power by force.

Speaking to journalists after meeting Austrian Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, Primakov was questioned about political stability in Russia as doctors met to decide when to operate on President Boris Yeltsin's heart.

"We have no doubt that at present unconstitutional methods of changing the situation at the helm are impossible. The country would not accept that, as shown by the results of the presidential election," Primakov said.
"There are grounds for believing that we are too far advanced on the road to constitutionalism and legality to be afraid of a violent seizure of power."

Worries about stability in Russia have increased recently because of Yeltsin's illness, the spectacular sacking of national security adviser Alexander Lebed, and signs of rising discontent in the armed forces over unpaid wages.
Russian trade unions are planning strikes and protest demonstrations on Tuesday November 5 against worsening delays in payments which have left millions of people without wages.
Early on Monday the defence ministry denied coup rumours which were circulating on foreign financial markets.
The reports appeared to stem from an article in the German newspaper Welt am Sonntag at the weekend about plans for joint protests by labour unions and army garrisons.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin visited airborne troops in Ryazan on Friday and promised to speed up payment of their wages. Defence Minister Igor Rodionov stressed the importance of unity when he addressed senior officers at the weekend.
In August 1991 senior officials attempted to seize power from Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev. Their coup attempt failed but the Soviet Union broke up four months later.

In October 1993 Yeltsin crushed an armed uprising in Moscow by his parliamentary opponents who tried to storm a television centre. Since then the capital has been calm although tens of thousands of people have died in fighting in Chechnya in the north Caucasus.
